title: Phrasal verbs 1: form and meaning
subtitle: find out, give up, pick up
summary: Understand how a verb plus an adverb or preposition makes a phrasal verb, and learn the most common ones.

lesson.heading: What a phrasal verb is
lesson.text: A phrasal verb is a verb + an adverb or a preposition, and sometimes a verb + an adverb **and** a preposition. The whole group works as one verb.

examples.text: He **fell over** and hurt his knee.
I'll try to **find out** the quickest way to get there.
He didn't like his coat, so he **gave** it **away**.
examples.note: = gave it to someone for no money

examples.text: Who's going to **sort out** the problem?
examples.note: = deal with it successfully, solve it

examples.text: He doesn't **get on with** his parents.
examples.note: = have a good relationship with. Verb + adverb + preposition.

lesson.heading: When the adverb adds almost nothing
lesson.text: With some verbs the adverb does not really change the meaning, and you can leave it out.

examples.text: I went to **lie (down)** on the bed.

lesson.heading: back = return
lesson.text: Sometimes the adverb adds one particular meaning to the verb. **Back** usually means return.

examples.text: I bought this jacket yesterday, but I'm going to **take** it **back** to the shop; it's too small.
You can look at the books, but remember to **put** them **back** on the shelf.
They liked Greece so much they want to **go back** next year.

lesson.heading: When the adverb changes the meaning
rows: give up
stop
My wife has decided to give up smoking.
carry on
continue
We'll take a short break and then carry on with the meeting.
put up
increase
The shops are going to put up the price of bread.
take on
employ
When the hotel gets busy, we have to take on more staff.
find out
learn, discover
I'll find out the quickest way to get there.
sort out
solve
Don't worry, I'll sort it out.
lesson.note: Give up does not mean the same as give, and carry on does not mean the same as carry.

lesson.heading: One phrasal verb, several meanings
lesson.text: Many phrasal verbs have more than one meaning. The situation tells you which meaning it is.

examples.text: I was busy, so I told him to **go away**.
We try to **go away** in August.
I **picked up** most of the rubbish.
I'm going to **pick** Jane **up** at the station.
examples.note: = collect someone, usually in a car

examples.text: Could you **put** the light **on**? Then I **put on** my best suit.
examples.note: put a machine on = switch it on; put clothes on = wear them

lesson.heading: Five meanings of go off
rows: leave a place and go somewhere else
Beatriz went off early; she had to meet a friend.
food is too old to eat
I think this meat has gone off.
a light or machine stops working
When the light goes off, the machine has finished.
a bomb or gun explodes
The bomb went off without any warning.
something suddenly starts making a noise
My alarm clock went off early this morning.

lesson.text: Do not learn phrasal verbs in long lists. Learn two or three at a time inside a short example sentence you can remember.

exercises.prompt: I can't see. Could you put the light ___?
exercises.explanation: Put a light on = switch it on.

exercises.prompt: It was broken, so I had to take it ___ to the shop.
I went to the airport to pick her ___.
exercises.explanation: Pick someone up = collect them, usually in a car.

exercises.prompt: I get married next year. I need to start saving ___.
exercises.explanation: Save up = keep money for something you want to buy.

exercises.prompt: Match each ordinary verb with a phrasal verb of similar meaning.
We'll have to ___ the price this year.
exercises.explanation: Put up a price = increase it.

exercises.prompt: We are planning to ___ ten new drivers next year.
Go off has several meanings. Match each sentence with the right one.

pairs.left: Beatriz went off early; she had to meet a friend.
I think this meat has gone off.
pairs.right: food is too old to eat

pairs.left: When the light goes off, the machine has finished.
pairs.right: a light or machine stops working

pairs.left: The bomb went off without any warning.
My alarm clock went off early this morning.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Is there still a problem? *B:* Don't worry. I'll ___ it out.
exercises.explanation: Sort something out = deal with it successfully.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Can we look at some books? *B:* Yes, but ___ them back afterwards.
exercises.explanation: Put something back = return it to its place.

exercises.prompt: *A:* What's the matter? *B:* I ___ and cut my knee.
exercises.hint: (two words, past = fall to the ground)
exercises.explanation: Fall over = fall to the ground.

exercises.prompt: *A:* ___ or we'll be late. *B:* OK, I'm coming.
exercises.explanation: Hurry up = be quick. The up can be left out.

exercises.prompt: Put the sentence in order. You are collecting Jane from the station in your car.
exercises.answer: I'm going to pick Jane up at the station.
alternatives: I'm going to pick up Jane at the station.
exercises.explanation: Pick someone up = collect them. The name can go before or after up.

exercises.statement: If you give up chocolate, it means you give your chocolate to another person.
exercises.explanation: Give up something = stop doing or eating it. Give something away = give it to someone for no money.
